title: Rebase vs merge, conflicts and safe force-pushes
objectives: Predict whether a merge fast-forwards or makes a merge commit, and explain what a rebase replays (`upstream..branch`, as new commits with new ids)
Resolve a conflict in a merge or a rebase — markers, `zdiff3`, `add` then `--continue` or `--abort` — knowing that `ours` and `theirs` swap during a rebase
Choose how `git pull` reconciles divergent branches (`--rebase`, `--ff-only`, a merge) and apply the golden rule: don't rebase commits others have
Force-push a rewritten branch with `--force-with-lease` plus `--force-if-includes`, and explain how a background fetch defeats a bare lease
Move a branch stacked on a squash-merged base with `rebase --onto`, and keep a stack current with `--update-refs`

sources.title: Pro Git: Basic Branching and Merging
Git 2.50 docs: git-rebase (the wording quoted in the readings)
git/git commit 031e2f7: "pull: abort by default when fast-forwarding is not possible" (first released in Git 2.33.1)
GitHub Docs: About comparing branches in pull requests

questions.prompt: Nobody has committed to `main` since you branched `feature` from it. You run `git switch main && git merge feature`. What happens?

options.text: A fast-forward: `main` moves to `feature`'s tip, and no new commit is made
A merge commit with two parents
`feature`'s commits are replayed onto `main` with new ids
A conflict, because both branches touch the same files

questions.explanation: `main` is an ancestor of `feature`, so there's nothing to combine — git just moves the `main` pointer forward (`Fast-forward` in the output). A merge commit appears only when both sides have commits the other lacks, or when you ask for one with `--no-ff`. Conflicts need *divergent* changes to the same lines.

questions.prompt: You rebased your already-pushed `feature` onto the latest `main`. Now `git push` is rejected as `non-fast-forward`. Why?

options.text: A rebase replays your commits as new commits with new ids, so the remote's `feature` is no longer an ancestor of yours
Someone pushed to `main` while you were rebasing
Remotes reject any branch that has been rebased
The rebase removed the branch's upstream setting

questions.explanation: A commit's id hashes its parent too, so replaying a commit onto a new parent makes a different commit. The remote still has the old ones, and a push may only move a branch forward. Pushing a rewritten branch needs a force — use `--force-with-lease`, so you don't overwrite commits you haven't seen.

questions.prompt: Mid-`git rebase main`, `config.txt` conflicts. You want **your feature branch's** version of the file. Which command takes it?

options.text: `git checkout --theirs config.txt`
`git checkout --ours config.txt`
`git checkout HEAD config.txt`
`git restore config.txt`

questions.explanation: A rebase checks out `main` and replays your commits onto it, so `HEAD` ("ours") is `main` plus what's been replayed so far, and "theirs" is the commit of yours being applied — the git-rebase docs: "the sides are swapped". In a merge it's the reverse. `checkout HEAD` also gives you `main`'s side. Then `git add config.txt` and `git rebase --continue`.

questions.prompt: `git pull` prints a list of `git config pull.…` hints and `fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.` What's going on?

options.text: The fetch worked; you and the remote both have new commits, and git won't pick merge or rebase for you
The fetch failed, so nothing was downloaded
The remote was force-pushed; you must reset to it
There's a merge conflict to resolve first

questions.explanation: `pull` is fetch + integrate. The fetch already updated `origin/main`; only integration stopped, because both sides moved and you haven't set `pull.rebase` or `pull.ff`. Git 2.27 began warning about this choice, and since Git 2.33.1 it refuses. Choose per pull (`--rebase`, `--no-rebase`, `--ff-only`) or once in config. No conflict has happened yet — nothing was merged.

questions.prompt: Which of these breaks the golden rule of rebasing?

options.text: Rebasing `main` onto a cleaned-up history and force-pushing it
`git pull --rebase` with two local commits you haven't pushed
Rebasing your own feature branch, which nobody else has checked out, onto `main`
`git rebase -i --autosquash` before opening your PR

questions.explanation: Pro Git: "Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on." Everyone has `main`; rewriting it leaves their clones holding the old commits, and a merge-style pull brings duplicates in. The other three rewrite only commits that nobody else has built on — which is what rebase is for.

questions.prompt: Alice rewrote her pushed `feature`. Bob pushed a fix to it an hour ago. Alice's editor auto-fetched since, and she runs `git push --force-with-lease`. What happens?

options.text: It succeeds and Bob's fix disappears from the remote — the fetch moved her `origin/feature` to include it
It's rejected with `(stale info)`, protecting Bob's fix
Git merges Bob's fix into her branch before pushing
Git asks her to confirm, showing Bob's commit

questions.explanation: The lease only checks that the remote is where Alice's `origin/feature` says it is. The background fetch updated `origin/feature` to Bob's commit, so the check passes even though Alice never looked at it. Adding `--force-if-includes` (or `push.useForceIfIncludes`) also requires that commit to be in her branch's reflog; here the push is rejected with `(remote ref updated since checkout)`.

questions.prompt: `feature-b` was stacked on `feature-a` (commits A1, A2). `feature-a` was **squash-merged** into `main`. On `feature-b`, `git rebase main` conflicts while applying A1. What's the right move?

options.text: `git rebase --abort`, then `git rebase --onto main feature-a` — replay only feature-b's own commits
Resolve each conflict by taking `main`'s side, A1 then A2
`git merge feature-a` into `feature-b` first
`git push --force-with-lease` to `main`

questions.explanation: The squash commit on `main` has A1+A2's changes but isn't A1 or A2, so `main..feature-b` still lists them and rebase tries to replay them onto code that already contains them. `--onto main feature-a` replays `feature-a..feature-b` — only B's commits — onto `main`. Resolving A1/A2's conflicts by hand can work, but it's slow and error-prone; merging `feature-a` in changes nothing about what `main` lacks.

questions.prompt: Same stack, but this time `main` merged `feature-a` with a **merge commit**. On `feature-b`, what does `git rebase main` replay?

options.text: Only feature-b's own commits — A1 and A2 are reachable from `main` through the merge's second parent
A1, A2 and feature-b's commits, like after a squash
feature-b's commits plus the merge commit
Nothing — the merge already brought feature-b in

questions.explanation: A merge commit keeps A1 and A2 in `main`'s history, so `main..feature-b` excludes them, and the rebase replays just B's commits. That's the difference from a squash merge, which leaves A1 and A2 out of `main`'s history. The merge commit itself belongs to `main`, so it's not replayed either.

prompts.prompt: You've fixed the conflict in `config.txt`. Mark it resolved and carry on with the rebase.
prompts.explanation: `git add` marks the file resolved (the `UU` in `git status` goes away). `--continue` finishes applying this commit and moves to the next one; a rebase can stop once per conflicting commit. `--abort` instead returns everything to how it was before the rebase.

prompts.prompt: Show the common ancestor between the two sides in every conflict (Git 2.35+).
prompts.explanation: `zdiff3` adds a `|||||||` section with the original text, so you can see what each side *changed* — not just two competing results. (`diff3` does the same with less trimming of common lines.)

prompts.prompt: Force-push your rebased branch without overwriting commits you've never had locally.
prompts.explanation: `--force-with-lease` refuses if the remote branch isn't where your remote-tracking branch says; `--force-if-includes` also refuses if that tip never made it into your local branch's reflog — the case a background fetch creates. `push.useForceIfIncludes true` turns the second one on by default.

prompts.prompt: After `feature-a` was squash-merged, move `feature-b` onto `main`, replaying only the commits after `feature-a`.
prompts.explanation: `git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch>` replays `upstream..branch` onto `newbase`. With the old base as `<upstream>`, its commits — already in `main` as the squash — are left out.

prompts.prompt: `main` moved under your stack (`feature-a` ← `feature-b`). From the top branch, rebase onto `main` and move `feature-a`'s pointer along with it (Git 2.38+).
prompts.explanation: `--update-refs` moves every local branch whose tip sits inside the replayed range — here `feature-a` — to its rewritten commit, and lists them: `Updated the following refs with --update-refs: refs/heads/feature-a`. Without it, `feature-a` would still point at the old commits. Then force-push each branch with `--force-with-lease`; `rebase.updateRefs true` makes this the default.

code: # feature-b = Base → A1 → A2 → B1 (stacked on feature-a = Base → A1 → A2)
git merge --squash feature-a && git commit -m "Feature A (#1)"
snippets.question: Which commits does the last command list?
snippets.answer: B1, A2 and A1 — all three
snippets.explanation: `main..feature-b` is "reachable from feature-b, not from main". The squash commit carries A1 and A2's *changes*, but it's a new commit with only `Base` as parent, so A1 and A2 aren't in `main`'s history. That's exactly the set `git rebase main` would try to replay — and why it conflicts.

code: git rebase main                 # stops on a conflict in config.txt
snippets.question: What does `cat` print?
snippets.explanation: During a rebase, `HEAD` is the branch being rebased onto (`main`, plus anything already replayed), so `--ours` is `main`'s `timeout = 45`. Your commit — the one being replayed — is `--theirs`. In a `git merge feature` from `main`, `--ours` would also be 45, but for the opposite reason: there, ours really is the branch you're on.

code: # feature-a was ONE commit (A1); main squash-merged it as "Feature A (#1)"
snippets.question: Does the rebase conflict? What's in the log afterwards?
snippets.answer: No conflict: git warns it skipped A1, and the log is B1, Feature A (#1), Base
acceptable: warning: skipped previously applied commit; B1 on top of the squash commit
snippets.explanation: Git prints `warning: skipped previously applied commit bb52381`: before replaying, rebase compares each commit's patch with the commits `main` gained, and the squash of a single commit is the same patch as that commit. With two or more commits in the base, the squash is one combined patch that matches none of them — and you're back to `--onto`.
